newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo financial markets stunned by BOJ survey.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo financial markets stunned by BOJ survey.

text.p: Japan's financial markets were stunned on Wednesday by a decline in business confidence in the Bank of Japan's (BOJ) quarterly "tankan" survey, where most forecasters had expected an improvement.

The survey of corporate sentiment pushed the yield of the benchmark 182nd 10-year JGBs below 3.00 percent at one point, for the first time since February, and also briefly drove the yen down against the dollar by more than 0.50 yen from the New York close.
The Tokyo stock market's key Nikkei index did not initially react to the data, but saw losses later in the day as concerns grew over the economy.

The survey's diffusion index for major manufacturers--an important gauge of business sentiment--dropped to minus seven from minus three in the previous survey in May. Forecasts by economists ranged from minus two to plus five.
The index represents the percentage of firms expecting business to improve minus those who expect it to worsen. The higher the number, the more optimistic the outlook.
Many dealers said the possibility of the Japanese central bank raising its discount rate this year had disappeared into thin air.
"A rate hike would have a negative impact, considering the risk of a breakdown in the current recovery," said a money trader at a European bank.
The BOJ slashed its official discount rate, at which it lends to commercial banks, to 0.5 percent last September to prevent the economy from sliding into recession.
When the survey was unveiled, the bond market rocketed, as buyers bought what little was offered.

"I don't know how high JGBs could go. The market will be underpinned by expectations that investors who have refrained from buying until the survey will be returning to the market finally," said a bond trader at a Japanese city bank.
At the shorter end of the yield curve, three-month Euroyen futures saw even more ferocious buying. The benchmark December contract jumped to 99.33 at one point from its pre-tankan level around 99.10.
The picture was the same in the foreign exchange market.

"Now that Japanese interest rates look like they'll stay at the current lows, possibly for the rest of the year, there won't be anyone buying the yen," said Yasuhito Kawashima, chief manager of foreign exchange at Toyo Trust & Banking Co.
The dollar/yen hit 108.35 at one point after the data, but eased back later. Kawashima expects the dollar to head for 109 yen although 108.50 yen will be an initial resistance level.

Kenneth Landon, senior currency strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, agreed: "I think this is a very positive sign for the dollar...This suggests that we will test 108.80 yen in the next few days and possibly break above into the 109s (yen level)".
But dealers also said the market's reaction was too drastic, particularly because of earlier talk in the market that the index might be at the top end of market expectations at plus five.
After the data was released, those who had gone short of bonds or dollars rushed to square their positions, a dealer said.
Although the initial market reaction was swift, a closer look into the survey would be necessary, some market players said. Many pointed out that most capital spending forecasts were revised upwards.

"Everyone was agitated by the headline figures at first, but capital spending was not so bad," said Yoshihiko Kaku, manager of the bond trading group at Mitsui Trust Securities Co Ltd. Big firms' capital spending in 1996/97 was seen up 6.6 percent year-on-year, revised upward from 6.0 percent in the previous survey, the BOJ said.
